messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 56
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Musician
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 71

He tells me he was twenty-three the first time it happened, a lifetime ago, but he can still feel the weight of the bass amplifier pressed into his ribs as he lay face-down on the grimy green carpet of a tour van. He was a session musician then, hungry, eager to prove himself. The bandleader—older, respected, a man he’d looked up to—offered him a ride home after the show. Instead, the van pulled into a dead-end alley behind a warehouse. The man’s hand landed on his thigh first, then moved higher. He says he froze. He didn’t scream, didn’t fight. He just lay there as the amplifier dug into his chest and the man’s breath, sour with whiskey, washed over his neck. Afterward, the bandleader drove him to his apartment and told him to keep his mouth shut if he wanted to work again. He never told anyone. He kept working. He kept playing.

Now he is fifty-six, a husband, a father of two grown daughters. He still plays bass in a local quartet—weddings, corporate events, the occasional jazz club. Music has always been his anchor. But over the past year, the anchor has started to drag. He describes it as a “short fuse,” a feeling of being constantly on edge. When a patron at a gig taps his shoulder to compliment a solo, he flinches so hard he nearly drops his instrument. He scans every room before he enters it, counting exits, noting who is standing too close. He has stopped drinking after shows—a choice he made deliberately, because a single beer now sends him into a spiral of nausea and flashbacks. The taste of whiskey, even on someone else’s breath, makes his stomach turn.

He wakes most nights around 3 a.m., drenched in sweat, the phantom pressure of that amplifier against his ribs. His wife tells him he’s been thrashing in his sleep, shouting things he doesn’t remember. He avoids the tour van memories by never renting a vehicle for the band; he insists they take separate cars. He avoids eye contact with older men in the audience, especially those with a certain swagger. He cannot explain why. The PCL-5 score of 71 reflects the depth of this avoidance—he has stopped going to the local music store where he used to browse strings, because the owner reminds him of the bandleader.

He says he feels “disconnected,” as though he is watching his own life from behind a dirty pane of glass. At his daughter’s wedding last summer, he stood at the altar with the bass, playing her requested song, but inside he was hollow, counting the seconds until he could leave. He has angry outbursts over small things—a misplaced guitar pick, a wrong note from the drummer—and then feels overwhelming shame. He has never told his wife about the assault. He says he doesn’t want to burden her, doesn’t want her to see him as broken. He believes he should have fought back, that a real man would have punched the man and walked away. Instead, he froze, and that frozen boy still lives inside him, a constant echo under every chord he plays.
